tb21_profile.skill: Train a text classifier to clear an accuracy floor on a hidden test set while staying under a hard artifact-size cap: format the data for the tool, tune hyperparameters, then compress/quantize to fit the budget
tb21_profile.domain: fastText CLI/python bindings, supervised text classification of Yelp reviews, NLP preprocessing and n-gram/embedding hyperparameters
tb21_profile.task_form: optimise-for-a-budget / model-training: iterate against a measured metric with two opposing constraints (accuracy >= 0.62, size < 150MB)

searches: tools.py search all "accuracy of at least|accuracy >|at least 0\.[0-9]|achieve.{0,20}accuracy"
tools.py search all "(accuracy|F1|AUC|R\^2|R2 score).{0,60}(at least|>=|exceed|greater than).{0,20}0\.[5-9]" -n 30
tools.py words all train model accuracy "test set" threshold -n 30

notes: Exactly one task in the whole pool mentions fastText (task_001191_5d4f858c, which builds the vendored library and uses a trained .bin), and nothing anywhere mentions quantization of a model for a size budget, so the size half of this task is essentially unrepresented; the nearest analogues are compress-to-a-budget tasks in other media (task_000510_7f94cbcf) and parameter-counting tasks. TMax is unusually strong here: it has a real cluster of 'iterate until an oracle metric clears a threshold' tasks that match the task_form exactly, which is the main thing worth training on. SWE-Smith has no supervised-learning repos at all; I used the charset/encoding detectors, which are genuine statistical text classifiers scored by accuracy, plus tokenisation tasks — judge those on skill, not form. SWE-Rebench's ML content (evalml, fuel, scikit-lego, mlxtend) is about training machinery rather than hitting a metric, so it stays around overall 2-3.
